title: Getting Paid for Molecular Tests: Coding, Coverage, Payment and FDA Status
summary: Separate the three questions behind every lab claim (coding, coverage and payment), see why Medicare’s payment rate is not the lab’s cost, and learn why a test without FDA clearance can still be billed while an in-house test built from analyte-specific reagents must carry a statement on its report.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 67 Hits 10 and 11 and Trap 3. Coding, coverage and pricing from the AMP Economics 101 report (Sireci 2020, full text via Europe PMC); fee schedule methods from 42 CFR 414.507 and 414.508; coverage exclusion from 42 CFR 411.15(k); report statement from 21 CFR 809.30(e); CLIA performance specifications from 42 CFR 493.1253 (all eCFR version 2026-10-01); LDT rule vacatur from the Federal Register final rule of 19 September 2025 (90 FR 45134, read via govinfo). The Social Security Act page at ssa.gov returned Access Denied and was not read. Qualifications recorded: the report statement is mandated for in-house tests built from analyte-specific reagents (rv-ch67-asr-report-statement-scope); billing without FDA clearance is allowed but coverage is a payer decision and some coverage policies depend on FDA status (rv-ch67-fda-billing-coverage-context); coverage, coding and payment are separate processes, not a strict sequence (rv-ch67-reimbursement-phases-order); US-only rules (rv-ch67-fda-payer-us-only). Not taught: Number Vault and figure items.

objectives: Distinguish coding, coverage and payment, and identify which one fails when a correctly coded claim is denied for medical necessity.
Explain how Medicare sets laboratory payment rates (weighted median of private-payer rates; crosswalk or gapfill for new codes) and why payment need not match cost.
Explain why lack of FDA clearance does not bar billing, what an in-house test built from analyte-specific reagents must state on its report, and what CLIA requires before such a test is used.

scenes.title: Two questions from billing
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a hospital molecular laboratory has built its own gene test from analyte-specific reagents (ASRs); the test is not FDA-cleared. The billing office asks two things. (1) “Without FDA clearance, are we even allowed to bill?” (2) “Last month a claim was denied even though the CPT code was correct. Why?” Question token: “Code, coverage, payment: where does the FDA fit?”

cues.text: A hospital lab has built its own gene test from analyte-specific reagents. The test has never been cleared by the FDA.
Billing asks: without FDA clearance, can we bill at all? And why was a claim denied when the code was correct?
Code, coverage and payment: where does the FDA fit in?

props.label: Code, coverage, payment: where is the FDA?

scenes.title: Three separate questions
scenes.altText: Three cards. CODING: the CPT code names the service performed; the ICD-10 code describes the diagnosis or clinical context and supports the claim. COVERAGE: does the payer consider the service reasonable and necessary for this patient? Medicare excludes services that are not reasonable and necessary for diagnosis or treatment; its coverage rules come from national coverage determinations (NCDs, written by CMS) and local coverage determinations (LCDs, issued by Medicare contractors; most molecular coverage decisions are LCDs), which pair a clinical scenario with ICD-10 and CPT codes. PAYMENT: the price the payer pays for that code. Note: once a code exists, its coverage and its pricing are set by separate processes.

cues.text: Getting paid for a test means answering three separate questions. Coding: the CPT code names the service, and the ICD-10 code describes the patient’s diagnosis or clinical situation.

Coverage: does the payer accept that this service is reasonable and necessary for this patient? Medicare spells this out in national and local coverage determinations, which pair a clinical scenario with ICD-10 and CPT codes.
Payment: how much the payer pays for that code. Once a code exists, its coverage and its price are decided by separate processes.
So a correct CPT code is not enough. The claim from the hook was denied at coverage: the diagnosis did not meet the coverage criteria.

props.label: Right code + uncovered diagnosis = coverage denial

scenes.title: Payment is not cost
scenes.altText: Medicare Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule card (42 CFR 414.507, from PAMA 2014): since 2018 the rate for most tests is the WEIGHTED MEDIAN of private-payer rates reported by applicable laboratories, weighted by volume; rates hold for three years for most tests (one year for advanced diagnostic laboratory tests). New-code card (42 CFR 414.508): CROSSWALK = use the rate of a comparable existing test; GAPFILL = when nothing is comparable, each Medicare contractor sets an amount from charges, resources needed to perform the test, other payers’ amounts and comparable tests; in the second year the median of the contractor amounts is paid. Conclusion token: the laboratory’s own cost is at most one input, so the payment can differ from what the test costs to run.

cues.text: Now the price. For most tests, Medicare’s lab fee schedule rate is the weighted median of what private payers paid laboratories, weighted by test volume. It is reset every three years for most tests.
A brand-new code is priced by crosswalk, borrowing the rate of a comparable existing test, or by gapfill when nothing is comparable.
In gapfill, each Medicare contractor weighs charges, the resources needed to run the test, and other payers’ rates; in year two, the median of those amounts is paid.
Either way, the lab’s own cost is at most one input. That is why a payment can bear little relation to what the test actually costs.

props.label: Lab cost = at most one input

scenes.title: Separate authorities: FDA, CLIA, payer
scenes.altText: Three authority cards. FDA (marketing of test kits and reagents): an in-house test built from analyte-specific reagents must carry on its report the statement required by 21 CFR 809.30(e): “This test was developed and its performance characteristics determined by (Laboratory Name). It has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.” The statement is not required when results come from the cleared or approved test. Status note: FDA’s May 2024 rule that would have treated laboratory-developed tests as devices was vacated by a federal court on 31 March 2025, and FDA reverted the regulation in September 2025. CLIA (lab quality, 42 CFR 493.1253(b)(2)): a lab that modifies a cleared test or introduces one not subject to clearance must establish accuracy, precision, analytical sensitivity, analytical specificity, reportable range and reference intervals before reporting patient results. PAYER (coverage and payment): Medicare contractors can cover laboratory-developed tests (for example through the MolDx program); as the AMP report describes it, Medicare’s 2018 national coverage decision for next-generation sequencing covered FDA-approved or cleared NGS companion diagnostic tests in advanced cancer and left NGS tests not approved by the FDA to local contractors. Hook answer card: yes, the test can be billed; whether it is paid depends on coverage; the report carries the ASR statement.

cues.text: Three authorities, three jobs. The FDA regulates test products. An in-house test built from analyte-specific reagents must say on its report that the lab developed it and that it has not been cleared or approved by the FDA.
A 2024 FDA rule said test products are devices even when a laboratory makes them, but a federal court vacated it in March 2025.

CLIA regulates lab quality. A test that is not FDA-cleared must have its own accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, reportable range and reference intervals established by the lab before it reports patient results.

Payers decide coverage and payment, and Medicare contractors can cover lab-developed tests. So, for the hook: yes, it can be billed; payment depends on coverage; and the report carries the required statement.

props.label: Hook: billable · paid if covered · statement on report

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “No FDA clearance, so the test cannot be billed” (✓ FDA regulates products; payers decide coverage and payment, and Medicare contractors can cover lab-developed tests; an ASR-built test carries the required report statement); “The CPT code is right, so the claim will be paid” (✓ coverage, meaning medical necessity for the documented diagnosis, is a separate question); “Medicare pays what the test costs” (✓ most rates are the weighted median of private-payer rates; new codes are crosswalked or gapfilled).

cues.text: Trap one: no FDA clearance means no billing. No: the FDA regulates products, payers decide payment, and an analyte-specific reagent test simply carries the required statement.
Trap two: the right code guarantees payment. No: coverage, meaning medical necessity for the documented diagnosis, is a separate question.
Trap three: Medicare pays what the test costs. No: most rates are a weighted median of private-payer rates, or a crosswalk or gapfill for new codes.

props.title: ✗ “No FDA clearance, no billing.”
lines: ✓ Payers decide; ASR test adds report statement

props.title: ✗ “Medicare pays the test’s cost.”
lines: ✓ Weighted median of private rates; crosswalk or gapfill

scenes.title: Name it, need it, number it
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “NAME it, NEED it, NUMBER it — and the FDA is not the cashier.” Coding names the service and diagnosis; coverage asks whether it was needed; payment puts a number on it. The FDA governs the product, not the payment. Tokens: Name = code · Need = coverage · Number = payment. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: name it, need it, number it, and the FDA is not the cashier. Coding names the service, coverage asks whether it was needed, payment puts a number on it.

Where it breaks: the three are not a strict one-way sequence; some coverage policies do depend on FDA status; the report statement rule is written for analyte-specific reagent tests; and all of this is US law.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Code (CPT + ICD-10) · coverage (reasonable and necessary) · payment (weighted median, crosswalk or gapfill)”, “FDA ≠ payer · ASR-built test: report statement · CLIA: lab establishes performance”.

cues.text: Getting paid for a molecular test needs a correct code, payer coverage for the documented diagnosis and a payment rate that need not match the lab’s cost, while FDA clearance is not a billing requirement, although an in-house test built from analyte-specific reagents must state on its report that the FDA has not cleared or approved it.

props.label: Code · coverage · payment (not the lab’s cost)
FDA ≠ payer · ASR test: report statement · CLIA validation

explanation.what: Plain language: to be paid, a lab must name the test correctly, the payer must agree the test was needed for this patient, and the payer then pays its own set price, which is not calculated from the lab’s costs. The FDA approves test products; it is not the body that decides payment. A lab’s own test that was not cleared by the FDA can still be billed, but if it was built from analyte-specific reagents (ASRs) the report must say the FDA has not cleared it. Scientific terms: CPT, ICD-10, coverage, reasonable and necessary, national coverage determination (NCD), local coverage determination (LCD), Medicare Administrative Contractor, MolDx, Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule, PAMA, weighted median, crosswalk, gapfill, analyte-specific reagent (ASR), laboratory-developed test (LDT), CLIA performance specifications.
explanation.why: Coding, coverage and pricing are run by different bodies through different processes, so each can fail independently. Payment rates come from market data and comparisons, not from each lab’s costs. FDA, CLIA and payers have separate legal jobs: product marketing, laboratory quality, and payment.
explanation.measure: Coverage: Medicare excludes services not reasonable and necessary for diagnosis or treatment (42 CFR 411.15(k)). Payment: weighted median of private-payer rates, reset every 3 years for most tests (414.507); new codes by crosswalk or gapfill (414.508). ASR-built in-house test: report statement required (21 CFR 809.30(e)). Test not subject to FDA clearance: lab establishes accuracy, precision, analytical sensitivity and specificity, reportable range and reference intervals (42 CFR 493.1253(b)(2)).
explanation.differs: Coding (what was done, for which diagnosis) vs coverage (was it needed) vs payment (how much); crosswalk (comparable test exists) vs gapfill (no comparable test); FDA clearance (product marketing) vs payer coverage; verification of a cleared test vs establishment of performance for a non-cleared test.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the failed phase when a medical-necessity denial occurs, decide whether a non-FDA-cleared test can be billed and what the report needs, or explain why payment differs from cost.

mnemonic.text: NAME it, NEED it, NUMBER it — and the FDA is not the cashier.
mnemonic.explanation: Name = coding (CPT plus ICD-10); Need = coverage (reasonable and necessary); Number = payment (the payer’s rate). The FDA governs products, not payment.
mnemonic.limitation: The three are not a strict one-way sequence; some coverage policies (such as Medicare’s national NGS decision) do depend on FDA status; the report statement rule is written for ASR-built tests; private payers differ; US rules only.

analogyLimitations: Regulatory text is paraphrased (US federal rules only); read the current regulations for exact wording.
Payment rules change yearly; the fee schedule phase-in and LDT policy are moving targets.
takeaway: Getting paid for a molecular test needs a correct code, payer coverage for the documented diagnosis and a payment rate that need not match the lab’s cost, while FDA clearance is not a billing requirement, although an in-house test built from analyte-specific reagents must state on its report that the FDA has not cleared or approved it.

questions.stem: A molecular test is coded with the correct CPT code, but the payer denies the claim because the documented diagnosis does not meet its medical-necessity criteria. Which part of reimbursement failed?

options.rationale: Correct. Coverage asks whether the service is reasonable and necessary for the patient’s clinical situation; coverage policies pair clinical scenarios with ICD-10 and CPT codes.
Incorrect. The CPT code was correct; the problem was whether the diagnosis justified the test.
Incorrect. Rate setting decides how much a covered code pays, not whether this claim qualifies.
Incorrect. The denial was for medical necessity, a payer decision, not an FDA product decision.

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory offers an in-house molecular test built from analyte-specific reagents. The test has not been cleared or approved by the FDA. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It can be billed, and the report must state that the lab developed the test and determined its performance and that the FDA has not cleared or approved it
options.rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 809.30(e) requires this statement for in-house tests built from ASRs; payment then depends on the payer’s coverage rules.

options.text: It cannot be billed until the FDA clears it
options.rationale: Incorrect. Payers decide coverage and payment; Medicare contractors can cover laboratory-developed tests.

options.text: It must always be billed under the unlisted code 81479
options.rationale: Incorrect. FDA status does not decide the code; the code depends on which test was performed.

options.text: No report statement is needed because the laboratory is CLIA-certified
options.rationale: Incorrect. CLIA certification does not replace the FDA report statement; CLIA separately requires the lab to establish the test’s performance specifications.

questions.stem: Since 2018, how is the Medicare Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule rate set for most existing laboratory tests?

options.text: The weighted median of private-payer rates reported by laboratories
options.rationale: Correct. 42 CFR 414.507 sets the rate at the volume-weighted median of private-payer rates, reset every three years for most tests.

options.text: Each laboratory’s documented cost plus a fixed margin
options.rationale: Incorrect. The lab’s own cost is not the basis of the rate, which is why payment can differ from cost.
Incorrect. Under 42 CFR 414.507 the rate is the weighted median of private-payer rates, not a figure set from what the laboratory charges.

options.text: A price set by the FDA when the test is cleared
options.rationale: Incorrect. The FDA does not set payment; CMS sets Medicare rates.

claims.text: Coding (CPT plus ICD-10), coverage (reasonable and necessary; NCDs and LCDs pairing clinical scenarios with codes) and payment are separate processes.
Weighted median of private-payer rates, three-year cycle for most tests; crosswalk and gapfill for new codes; lab cost at most one input.
Report statement for in-house tests built from analyte-specific reagents; not required when the cleared test is used.

Medicare contractors can cover laboratory-developed tests (MolDx); the 2018 national NGS coverage decision (as described by AMP) covered FDA-approved or cleared NGS companion diagnostics in advanced cancer and left other NGS tests to contractors.
CLIA establishment of performance specifications for tests not subject to FDA clearance.
2024 LDT rule vacated March 2025; regulation reverted September 2025.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 67 Hit 11 and Trap 3 say any test not cleared by the FDA must carry a report disclaimer. The federal rule found (21 CFR 809.30(e)) requires a specific statement for in-house tests developed using analyte-specific reagents, and says it is not required when results come from the cleared or approved test. The lesson teaches the ASR rule and its wording (register flag rv-ch67-asr-report-statement-scope).

Ch. 67 Hit 11 and Trap 3 are right that FDA clearance is not a billing requirement, but whether a non-cleared test is paid depends on payer coverage, and some coverage policies depend on FDA status (as the AMP report describes it, Medicare’s 2018 NGS national coverage decision covered FDA-approved or cleared NGS companion diagnostics in advanced cancer and left NGS tests not approved by the FDA to local contractors). Non-cleared tests also need CLIA establishment of performance specifications (register flag rv-ch67-fda-billing-coverage-context).

Ch. 67 Hit 10 presents reimbursement as a sequence coverage → coding → payment. The AMP report describes code creation first, then separate processes for coverage and pricing, and coverage policies are written in terms of ICD-10 and CPT codes; the lesson teaches three separate questions rather than a fixed order (register flag rv-ch67-reimbursement-phases-order).

FDA, CLIA and Medicare payment rules are US federal systems, and US LDT policy changed in 2024 and 2025. Philippine regulation and reimbursement are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local rules (register flag rv-ch67-fda-payer-us-only).
